Write the first page of an onboarding document for a new backend engineer joining a payments team. Around 200 words.

# Welcome to Payments

## What this team owns

We move money. Every service in this repo touches a real ledger entry, which means a bug here shows up in someone's bank account, not in a dashboard.

Three systems make up the core:

The authorization service talks to card networks. It holds funds, releases holds, and answers in under 300ms or the network times us out.

The ledger records every movement as a double-entry pair. It is append-only. Nothing gets updated in place, ever. If a number is wrong, you write a correcting entry.

The settlement pipeline runs nightly, batches captured payments by merchant, and files them with our banking partners.

## Your first week

Read `docs/idempotency.md` before you write any code. Every write endpoint we own takes an idempotency key, and the reason is that networks retry, clients retry, and our own queues retry. A payment that runs twice is the failure mode we spend most of our time preventing.

Then pair with your onboarding buddy on a real ticket from the `payments-starter` queue. These are small and scoped, but they ship to production.

## Two things to know now

You will get paged. The rotation starts in week three, and someone senior shadows your first two shifts.

Money bugs get escalated immediately, without waiting to confirm the diagnosis. Say something in `#payments-oncall` the moment you suspect one. Nobody has ever been criticized here for raising a false alarm.

## Who to ask for what

Ask in the open channel first. Someone usually answers faster than a direct message, and the answer gets logged where the next new hire can find it.

`#payments-eng` covers anything about the three core systems, code review questions, and "is this behavior expected." Priya owns the authorization service and knows the card network quirks nobody wrote down. Marcus owns the ledger and reviews every schema change to it, so tag him before you open that pull request.

`#payments-oncall` handles anything happening right now. Suspected money bugs, alerts firing, a merchant reporting a missing settlement.

For banking partner behavior, settlement timing, or why a batch got rejected, ask Dana in `#partner-ops`. She talks to the partners directly and can tell you whether a delay is ours or theirs.

For access, credentials, or a staging environment that will not come up, file a ticket in the platform queue rather than asking here. We do not own that infrastructure and cannot fix it faster than they can.

Your manager handles scope, priorities, and anything about the ticket you were handed. If you are stuck for more than half a day, that is the conversation to have, and having it early is the expected behavior here.
